outline_elements.rule: English Language is placed in Year 1 general education; workplace and management elements (Customer and Personal Service, Administrative, Clerical, Administration and Management, Personnel and Human Resources, Education and Training) get no course slot unless the major's CIP series is about them; the next three elements go to Year 2 and up to three more (ordered by importance to the entry targets) to Year 3; if fewer than two remain for Year 3, knowledge rated at least 2.5 for the entry targets fills it

method.supervisory_tasks: task statement matches a supervisory/managerial pattern (supervise, provide supervision, direct and coordinate, direct the work/activities/staff of, manage staff/personnel/employees/workers/teams, oversee the work/staff, hire, subordinates, assign work to, evaluate the work/performance of, train and supervise); 'under supervision' does not count

quality_flags.note: Authored tier: entry targets and practice tasks were chosen and reviewed per major, so the generated-tier plausibility flags are not applied. Informational only: cited tasks whose O*NET statement is supervisory are listed; their authored scenarios say when they are practice for a later or graduate role.

entry_target_basis: Job Zone 4 linked occupations (excluding Manager/Chief/Postsecondary/All Other/Supervisor/Director/Treasurers and Controllers titles), ranked by similarity of their O*NET knowledge-importance profile to the average profile of the eligible linked occupations (Pearson correlation), base O*NET-SOC .00 codes first; then a documented DreamCo manual override (authored/target_overrides.json) changed the rule output (17-2011.00, 17-2141.00, 13-1051.00) to 17-2141.00, 17-2011.00, 17-2141.02

entry_target_review.reason: Mechanical Engineers is placed first as the degree's primary occupation (the rule ranked Aerospace Engineers first). Cost Estimators was replaced by Automotive Engineers, a mechanical-engineering specialty that is a more direct engineering entry role; cost estimating remains a valid alternative.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. You are the junior engineer leading a five-person team (two design engineers, a composites technician, a test technician and an instrumentation intern) through a static load test of a new carbon-fiber wing spar for a small uncrewed aircraft. The test must show the spar carries 1.5 times the limit load without failure. Write the coordination plan for the three-week campaign: who does what, the sequence from specimen fabrication to test report, the safety controls for loading to failure, the instrumentation plan, and how you handle a schedule slip if the first specimen has a manufacturing flaw.

rubric.description: Each person's responsibilities and handoffs are explicit, and the sequence (fabricate, inspect, instrument, test, analyze, report) is logical.
Instrumentation (strain gauges, load cells, deflection) and load steps are appropriate for verifying the 1.5 factor, with predicted values to compare against.
Includes test-area exclusion zones and stop criteria, and a realistic fallback for a flawed specimen.

reference_answer_outline: Week 1: fabricate two specimens, ultrasonic or visual inspection, strain gauge placement plan.
Week 2: test-rig checkout, calibration of load cell, dry run at low load, test-readiness review.
Week 3: incremental loading to limit load, then to 1.5 times, holding and recording; optional test to failure.
Safety: shields, exclusion zone, abort criteria on unexpected strain or cracking sounds.
Contingency: second specimen built in parallel; report delays communicated with a revised date.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. Use a publicly available mechanical drawing of a machined bracket or shaft (or sketch an invented one with at least one hole pattern, a tolerance block, a surface-finish note and two geometric tolerances such as position and flatness). Write a review memo for the machine shop: explain in plain words what each critical dimension and geometric tolerance requires, identify the datum features and how the part would be fixtured for inspection, flag any ambiguity or missing information, and list questions you would ask the designer before release.

rubric.description: Geometric tolerances, datums, tolerance block and surface-finish notes are interpreted correctly.
Links requirements to how the part is made and inspected (fixturing on datums, measurement method).
Identifies real gaps or conflicts in the drawing and turns them into specific questions.

reference_answer_outline: Datum A primary face, B and C as hole or edge features; part located on these for inspection.
Position tolerance on the hole pattern relative to A, B, C explained as a tolerance zone; flatness on the mounting face.
Default tolerances from the title block apply to unlabeled dimensions.
Ambiguities such as missing material spec, unclear thread callout or conflicting dimensions.
Questions for the designer and a recommendation to fix before release.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. Invented case: warranty data show a compact car's rear wheel bearings failing at about 30,000 km in one region, three times the normal rate, starting with vehicles built after a supplier change in March. Write a root-cause analysis using a structured method (such as 8D, fishbone and five whys): the problem statement, containment actions, the candidate causes across material, process, design and usage, the data and teardown tests you would request to confirm or rule out each, and how you will verify the permanent fix.

rubric.description: Uses a recognized method with a clear problem statement (what, where, when, how many) and containment.
Candidate causes are specific and each has a test or data check to confirm or eliminate it, rather than jumping to conclusions.
The permanent fix is verified with tests or field data and the process is changed to prevent recurrence.

reference_answer_outline: Problem statement with build dates, region, mileage and failure rate.
Containment: inspect stock from the new supplier, quarantine suspect lots.
Causes: seal design letting in road salt (region), heat treatment change at the supplier, press-fit tolerance at assembly.
Checks: teardown of failed parts for corrosion versus fatigue, hardness tests, compare press-fit force logs.
Verify fix with accelerated life testing and monitor warranty claims for six months.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. A customer needs a quadcopter arm made of an aluminum tube that is 250 mm long, carries a 1.2 kg motor thrust at the tip, and must deflect less than 3 mm with a safety factor of 2 on yield. Build a simple analytical model (cantilever beam) to size the tube's outer diameter and wall thickness, show the equations and numbers, compare two candidate tube sizes, then explain how you would check the hand calculation with finite-element analysis and what extra effects (vibration, fatigue, joint stiffness) the simple model misses.

rubric.description: Uses correct cantilever bending stress and deflection relations with consistent units and a stated material property.
Compares candidates against both requirements and chooses one with mass considered.
Explains how FEA or testing would validate the model and names the missing effects with their likely impact.

reference_answer_outline: Load about 11.8 N; moment at root is load times 0.25 m.
Stress from bending moment times outer radius divided by second moment of area; deflection from load times length cubed over 3 E I.
Two tube sizes tabulated with stress, safety factor, deflection and mass.
FEA with matching boundary conditions; mesh check; compare with hand result within a few percent.
Missing effects: motor vibration and resonance, fatigue at the clamp, clamp compliance.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. Invented case: a hospital's chilled-water system keeps tripping one of two chillers on low refrigerant pressure during hot afternoons, and the operating rooms are drifting above their temperature limit. You are the mechanical engineer meeting the facilities supervisor and the chiller service technician. Write a meeting script and follow-up note: what information you ask for (trend logs, alarm history, condenser water temperatures), likely causes you will discuss, the interim operating procedure to protect the operating rooms, and the agreed next steps.

rubric.description: Asks for specific data and observations that would distinguish likely causes rather than guessing.
Discusses plausible causes (fouled condenser, low charge, failing expansion valve, cooling tower performance) correctly.
Defines a safe interim procedure for critical spaces and clear next steps with owners and dates.

reference_answer_outline: Request: alarm times, suction and discharge pressures, condenser water supply temperature, recent service history.
Likely causes include a refrigerant leak, a faulty expansion valve or poor heat rejection on hot days.
Interim procedure: stage the healthy chiller first, pre-cool operating rooms in the morning, portable cooling backup.
Next steps: leak test, condenser tube inspection, cooling tower check; owners and dates.
Follow-up note circulated the same day with decisions recorded.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. Your team is considering replacing a stamped-steel battery-tray bracket in an electric vehicle with a die-cast aluminum version to save mass. Write a short engineering specification for the new bracket (loads, crash and vibration requirements, corrosion protection, mass target, interface dimensions) and a rough per-unit cost estimate for both designs at 100,000 vehicles per year, including material, processing, tooling amortization and joining. State your assumptions and recommend whether to proceed.

rubric.description: Requirements are quantified and verifiable (load values, test standards, mass limit, interface tolerances).
The estimate separates material, process, tooling amortization and assembly with stated assumptions and correct arithmetic.
Weighs mass savings against cost, galvanic corrosion and supply risk and gives a clear decision.

reference_answer_outline: Specification: static and crash loads, vibration profile, salt-spray requirement, mass under a target, bolt pattern tolerances.
Steel: low material cost, cheap stamping, welding cost; aluminum: higher material cost, die-casting tooling amortized over volume.
Assumptions for prices per kilogram, cycle times and tooling cost.
Cost per kilogram of mass saved compared with the program's target.
Recommendation with risks such as dissimilar-metal joints.
